Lie symmetry analysis of nonlinear evolution equation for description nonlinear waves in a viscoelastic tube

Mehdi Nadjafikhah ††thanks: Corresponding author: Department of Mathematics, Islamic Azad University, Karaj Branch, Karaj, Iran. e-mail: m_nadjafikhah@iust.ac.ir    Vahid Shirvani-Sh ††thanks: e-mail: v.shirvani@kiau.ac.ir
Abstract

In this paper, the Lie symmetry method is performed for the nonlinear evolution equation for description nonlinear waves in a viscoelastic tube. we will find one and two-dimensional optimal system of Lie subalgebras. Furthermore, preliminary classification of its group-invariant solutions are investigated.

Keywords. Lie symmetry, Optimal system, Group-invariant solutions, Nonlinear evolution equation.

1 Introduction

The theory of Lie symmetry groups of differential equations was developed by Sophus Lie [10]. Such Lie groups are invertible point transformations of both the dependent and independent variables of the differential equations. The symmetry group methods provide an ultimate arsenal for analysis of differential equations and is of great importance to understand and to construct solutions of differential equations. Several applications of Lie groups in the theory of differential equations were discussed in the literature, the most important ones are: reduction of order of ordinary differential equations, construction of invariant solutions, mapping solutions to other solutions and the detection of linearizing transformations (for many other applications of Lie symmetries see [11], [2] and [1]).

In the present paper, we study the following fifth-order nonlinear evolution equation

ut+a​u​ux+b​ux3+c​ux4+d​ux5=e​ux2.\displaystyle u_{t}+auu_{x}+bu_{x^{3}}+cu_{x^{4}}+du_{x^{5}}=eu_{x^{2}}. (1)

where aa,bb,cc,dd and ee are positive constants. This equation was introduced recently by Kudryashov and Sinelshchikov [8] which is the generalization of the famous Kawahara equation. By using the reductive perturbation method, they obtained the equation (1). Study of nonlinear wave processes in viscoelastic tube is the important problem such tubes similar to large arteries (see [4],[9] and [3]).

In this paper, by using the lie point symmetry method, we will investigate the equation (1) and looking the representation of the obtained symmetry group on its Lie algebra. We will find the preliminary classification of group-invariant solutions and then we can reduce the equation (1) to an ordinary differential equation.

This work is organized as follows. In section 2 we recall some results needed to construct Lie point symmetries of a given system of differential equations. In section 3, we give the general form of a infinitesimal generator admitted by equation (1) and find transformed solutions. Section 4, is devoted to the construction of the group-invariant solutions and its classification which provides in each case reduced forms of equation (1).

2 Method of Lie Symmetries

In this section, we recall the general procedure for determining symmetries for any system of partial differential equations (see [11] and [2]). To begin, let us consider the general case of a nonlinear system of partial differential equations of order nnth in pp independent and qq dependent variables is given as a system of equations

Δν(x,u(n))=0,ν=1,⋯,l,\displaystyle\Delta_{\nu}(x,u^{(n)})=0,\;\;\;\;\;\nu=1,\cdots,l, (2)

involving x=(x1,⋯,xp)x=(x^{1},\cdots,x^{p}), u=(u1,⋯,uq)u=(u^{1},\cdots,u^{q}) and the derivatives of uu with respect to xx up to nn, where u(n)u^{(n)} represents all the derivatives of uu of all orders from 00 to nn. We consider a one-parameter Lie group of infinitesimal transformations acting on the independent and dependent variables of the system (2)

x~i\displaystyle\tilde{x}^{i} =\displaystyle= xi+sξi(x,u)+O(s2),i=1⋯,p,\displaystyle x^{i}+s\xi^{i}(x,u)+O(s^{2}),\hskip 28.45274pti=1\cdots,p,
u~j\displaystyle\tilde{u}^{j} =\displaystyle= uj+sηj(x,u)+O(s2),j=1⋯,q,\displaystyle u^{j}+s\eta^{j}(x,u)+O(s^{2}),\hskip 25.60747ptj=1\cdots,q,

where ss is the parameter of the transformation and ξi\xi^{i}, ηj\eta^{j} are the infinitesimals of the transformations for the independent and dependent variables, respectively. The infinitesimal generator 𝐯{\mathbf{v}} associated with the above group of transformations can be written as

𝐯=∑i=1pξi(x,u)∂xi+∑j=1qηj(x,u)∂uj.\displaystyle{\mathbf{v}}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\xi^{i}(x,u)\partial_{x^{i}}+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\eta^{j}(x,u)\partial_{u^{j}}. (4)

A symmetry of a differential equation is a transformation which maps solutions of the equation to other solutions. The invariance of the system (2) under the infinitesimal transformations leads to the invariance conditions (Theorem 2.36 of [11])

Pr(n)𝐯[Δν(x,u(n))]=0,ν=1,⋯,l,wheneverΔν(x,u(n))=0,\displaystyle\textrm{Pr}^{(n)}{\mathbf{v}}\big[\Delta_{\nu}(x,u^{(n)})\big]=0,\;\;\;\;\;\nu=1,\cdots,l,\;\;\;\;\mbox{whenever}\;\;\;\;\;\Delta_{\nu}(x,u^{(n)})=0, (5)

where Pr(n)\textrm{Pr}^{(n)} is called the nt​hn^{th} order prolongation of the infinitesimal generator given by

Pr(n)𝐯=𝐯+∑α=1q∑JφαJ(x,u(n))∂uJα,\displaystyle\textrm{Pr}^{(n)}{\mathbf{v}}={\mathbf{v}}+\sum^{q}_{\alpha=1}\sum_{J}\varphi^{J}_{\alpha}(x,u^{(n)})\partial_{u^{\alpha}_{J}}, (6)

where J=(j1,⋯,jk)J=(j_{1},\cdots,j_{k}), 1≤jk≤p1\leq j_{k}\leq p, 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n and the sum is over all JJ’s of order 0<#​J≤n0<\#J\leq n. If #​J=k\#J=k, the coefficient φJα\varphi_{J}^{\alpha} of ∂uJα\partial_{u_{J}^{\alpha}} will only depend on kk-th and lower order derivatives of uu, and

φαJ​(x,u(n))=DJ​(φα−∑i=1pξi​uiα)+∑i=1pξi​uJ,iα,\displaystyle\varphi_{\alpha}^{J}(x,u^{(n)})=D_{J}(\varphi_{\alpha}-\sum_{i=1}^{p}\xi^{i}u_{i}^{\alpha})+\sum_{i=1}^{p}\xi^{i}u^{\alpha}_{J,i}, (7)

where uiα:=∂uα/∂xiu_{i}^{\alpha}:=\partial u^{\alpha}/\partial x^{i} and uJ,iα:=∂uJα/∂xiu_{J,i}^{\alpha}:=\partial u_{J}^{\alpha}/\partial x^{i}.

One of the most important properties of these infinitesimal symmetries is that they form a Lie algebra under the usual Lie bracket.

We consider the one parameter Lie group of infinitesimal transformations on (x1=x,x2=t,u1=u)(x^{1}=x,x^{2}=t,u^{1}=u),

x~\displaystyle\tilde{x} =\displaystyle= x+s​ξ​(x,t,u)+O⁡(s2),\displaystyle x+s\xi(x,t,u)+O(s^{2}),
t~\displaystyle\tilde{t} =\displaystyle= x+s​η​(x,t,u)+O⁡(s2),\displaystyle x+s\eta(x,t,u)+O(s^{2}), (8)
u~\displaystyle\tilde{u} =\displaystyle= x+s​φ​(x,t,u)+O⁡(s2),\displaystyle x+s\varphi(x,t,u)+O(s^{2}),

𝐯=ξ(x,t,u)∂x+η(x,t,u)∂t+φ(x,t,u)∂u.\displaystyle{\mathbf{v}}=\xi(x,t,u)\partial_{x}+\eta(x,t,u)\partial_{t}+\varphi(x,t,u)\partial_{u}. (9)

and, by (6) its third prolongation is

⋯+φt2∂ut2+φx​t4∂ux​t4+φt5∂ut5.\displaystyle\cdots+\varphi^{t^{2}}\,\partial_{u_{t^{2}}}+\varphi^{xt^{4}}\,\partial_{u_{xt^{4}}}+\varphi^{t^{5}}\,\partial_{u_{t^{5}}}.

where, for instance by (7) we have

φx\displaystyle\varphi^{x} =\displaystyle= Dx​(φ−ξ​ux−η​ut)+ξ​ux2+η​ux​t,\displaystyle D_{x}(\varphi-\xi\,u_{x}-\eta\,u_{t})+\xi\,u_{x^{2}}+\eta\,u_{xt},
φt\displaystyle\varphi^{t} =\displaystyle= Dt​(φ−ξ​ux−η​ut)+ξ​ux​t+η​ut2,\displaystyle D_{t}(\varphi-\xi\,u_{x}-\eta\,u_{t})+\xi\,u_{xt}+\eta\,u_{t^{2}}, (11)
…\displaystyle\ldots
φt5\displaystyle\varphi^{t^{5}} =\displaystyle= Dx5​(φ−ξ​ux−η​ut)+ξ​ux5​t+η​ut5,\displaystyle D^{5}_{x}(\varphi-\xi\,u_{x}-\eta\,u_{t})+\xi\,u_{x^{5}t}+\eta\,u_{t^{5}},

where DxD_{x} and DtD_{t} are the total derivatives with respect to xx and tt respectively. By (5) the vector field 𝐯{\mathbf{v}} generates a one parameter symmetry group of equation (1) if and only if

Pr(5)​𝐯​[ut+a​u​ux+b​ux3+c​ux4+d​ux5−e​ux2]=0,wheneverut+a​u​ux+b​ux3+c​ux4+d​ux5−e​ux2=0.\displaystyle\left.\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle\textrm{Pr}^{(5)}{\mathbf{v}}[u_{t}+auu_{x}+bu_{x^{3}}+cu_{x^{4}}+du_{x^{5}}-eu_{x^{2}}]=0,\\[14.22636pt] \displaystyle\mbox{whenever}\hskip 14.22636ptu_{t}+auu_{x}+bu_{x^{3}}+cu_{x^{4}}+du_{x^{5}}-eu_{x^{2}}=0.\end{array}\right.

The condition (3) is equivalent to

a​ux​φ+a​u​φx+φt−e​φx2+b​φx3+c​φx4+d​φx5=0,wheneverut+a​u​ux+b​ux3+c​ux4+d​ux5−e​ux2=0.\displaystyle\left.\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle au_{x}\varphi+au\varphi^{x}+\varphi^{t}-e\varphi^{x^{2}}+b\varphi^{x^{3}}+c\varphi^{x^{4}}+d\varphi^{x^{5}}=0,\\[14.22636pt] \displaystyle\mbox{whenever}\hskip 14.22636ptu_{t}+auu_{x}+bu_{x^{3}}+cu_{x^{4}}+du_{x^{5}}-eu_{x^{2}}=0.\end{array}\right.

Substituting (11) into (3), and equating the coefficients of the various monomials in partial derivatives with respect to xx and various power of uu, we can find the determining equations for the symmetry group of the equation (1). Solving this equation, we get the following forms of the coefficient functions

ξ=c2​a​t+c3,η=c1,φ=c2.\displaystyle\xi=c_{2}at+c_{3},\quad\eta=c_{1},\quad\varphi=c_{2}. (18)

where c1c_{1}, c2c_{2} and c3c_{3} are arbitrary constant. Thus, the Lie algebra of infinitesimal symmetry of the equation (1) is spanned bye the three vector fields:

v1=∂x,v2=∂t,v3=t∂x+1a∂u.\displaystyle\textbf{v}_{1}=\partial_{x},\quad\textbf{v}_{2}=\partial_{t},\quad\textbf{v}_{3}=t\,\partial_{x}+\frac{1}{a}\partial_{u}. (19)

4 Optimal system and invariant solution of (1)

In this section, we obtain the optimal system and reduced forms of the equation (1) by using symmetry group properties obtained in previous section. Since the original partial differential equation has two independent variables, then this partial differential equation transform into the ordinary differential equation after reduction.

Definition 4.1

Let GG be a Lie group with Lie algebra 𝔤{g}. An optimal system of s−s-parameter subgroups is a list of conjugacy inequivalent s−s-parameter subalgebras with the property that any other subgroup is conjugate to precisely one subgroup in the list. Similarly, a list of s−s-parameter subalgebras forms an optimal system if every s−s-parameter subalgebra of 𝔤{g} is equivalent to a unique member of the list under some element of the adjoint representation: 𝔥¯=A​d​(g⁡(𝔥))\overline{{h}}={\mathrm{A}d}(g({{h}})).[11]

Theorem 4.2

Let HH and H¯\overline{H} be connected s-dimensional Lie subgroups of the Lie group GG with corresponding Lie subalgebras 𝔥{h} and 𝔥¯\overline{{h}} of the Lie algebra 𝔤{g} of GG. Then H¯\overline{H}=g​H​g−1gHg^{-1} are conjugate subgroups if and only if 𝔥¯=A​d​(g⁡(𝔥))\overline{{h}}={\mathrm{A}d}(g({{h}})) are conjugate subalgebras. [11]

By theorem (4.2), the problem of finding an optimal system of subgroups is equivalent to that of finding an optimal system of subalgebras. For one-dimensional subalgebras, this classification problem is essentially the same as the problem of classifying the orbits of the adjoint representation, since each one-dimensional subalgebra is determined by nonzero vector in 𝔤{g}. This problem is attacked by the naïve approach of taking a general element 𝐕{\mathbf{V}} in 𝔤{g} and subjecting it to various adjoint transformation so as to ”simplify” it as much as possible. Thus we will deal with th construction of the optimal system of subalgebras of 𝔤{g}.

To compute the adjoint representation, we use the Lie series

A​d​(exp⁡(ε​𝐯i)​𝐯j)=𝐯j−ε⁡[𝐯i,𝐯j]+ε22​[𝐯i,[𝐯i,𝐯j]]−⋯,\displaystyle{\mathrm{A}d}(\exp(\varepsilon{\mathbf{v}}_{i}){\mathbf{v}}_{j})={\mathbf{v}}_{j}-\varepsilon[{\mathbf{v}}_{i},{\mathbf{v}}_{j}]+\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}[{\mathbf{v}}_{i},[{\mathbf{v}}_{i},{\mathbf{v}}_{j}]]-\cdots, (23)

where [𝐯i,𝐯j][{\mathbf{v}}_{i},{\mathbf{v}}_{j}] is the commutator for the Lie algebra, ε\varepsilon is a parameter, and i,j=1,2,3i,j=1,2,3. Then we have the Table 2.

for certain scalar a′′1{a^{\prime\prime}}_{1}. Similarly we can vanish a′′1{a^{\prime\prime}}_{1}, so every one-dimensional subalgebra generated by a 𝐕{\mathbf{V}} with a3=0a_{3}=0 is equivalent to the subalgebra spanned by v2\textbf{v}_{2}.                                 □\mathchar 1027\relax

Theorem 4.4

An optimal system of two-dimensional Lie algebras of the equation (1) is provided by

<αv2+v3,βv1+γv3><\alpha\textbf{v}_{2}+\textbf{v}_{3},\beta\textbf{v}_{1}+\gamma\textbf{v}_{3}>

Symmetry group method will be applied to the (1) to be connected directly to some order differential equations. To do this, a particular linear combinations of infinitesimals are considered and their corresponding invariants are determined.

The equation (1) is expressed in the coordinates (x,t,u)(x,t,u), so to reduce this equation is to search for its form in specific coordinates. Those coordinates will be constructed by searching for independent invariants (χ,ζ)(\chi,\zeta) corresponding to the infinitesimal generator. So using the chain rule, the expression of the equation in the new coordinate allows us to the reduced equation.

In what follows, we begin the reduction process of equation (1).

4.5 Galilean-Invariant Solutions.

First, consider v3=t∂x+1a∂u\textbf{v}_{3}=t\,\partial_{x}+\frac{1}{a}\partial_{u}. To determine independent invariants II, we need to solve the first partial differential equations vi\textbf{v}_{i}(I)=0, that is invariants ζ\zeta and χ\chi can be found by integrating the corresponding characteristic system, which is

d​t0=d​xt=a​d​u1.\displaystyle\frac{dt}{0}=\frac{dx}{t}=\frac{a\,du}{1}. (27)

The obtained solution are given by

χ=t,ζ=u−xa​t.\displaystyle\chi=t,\qquad\zeta=u-\frac{x}{a\,t}. (28)

Therefore, a solution of our equation in this case is

u=f⁡(x,χ,ζ)=ζ+xa​t.\displaystyle u=f(x,\chi,\zeta)=\zeta+\frac{x}{a\,t}. (29)

The derivatives of uu are given in terms of ζ\zeta and χ\chi as

ux=1a​t,ux2=ux3=ux4=ux5=0,ut=ζχ−1a​t2​x.\displaystyle u_{x}=\frac{1}{a\,t},\quad u_{x^{2}}=u_{x^{3}}=u_{x^{4}}=u_{x^{5}}=0,\quad u_{t}=\zeta_{\chi}-\frac{1}{a\,t^{2}}\,x. (30)

Substituting (30) into the equation (1), we obtain the order ordinary differential equation

ζχ+1χ​ζ=0.\displaystyle\zeta_{\chi}+\frac{1}{\chi}\,\zeta=0. (31)

The solution of this equation is ζ=c1χ\zeta=\frac{c_{1}}{\chi}. Consequently, we obtain that

u⁡(x,t)=x+a​c1a​t.\displaystyle u(x,t)=\frac{x+a\,c_{1}}{a\,t}. (32)

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
